summary: Protect your health and productivity by folding light, sustained exercise into time you already spend playing, and don't overdo it.
takeaways: Pedal an exercise bike while gaming so exercise breezes by
Racing games suit pedaling; stealth games make you slow down
Exercisers tend to be far more productive; do a little
Don't overdo it; ramp up gradually

principles.principle: Pair play sessions with sustained aerobic exercise, like an exercise bike.
principles.why: Playing takes your mind off the effort, so long sessions that would be tough breeze by, and aerobic exercise works best when sustained; he has pedaled for two hours.
principles.how: Set up an exercise bike, stepper or treadmill in front of the screen and pedal through play sessions; racing games work well when pedaling feels like going faster.
principles.anti_pattern: Pairing it with stealth games, where you unconsciously pedal slower.
principles.example: Sakurai's own exercise-bike gaming sessions of up to two hours.
principles.quote: But pedaling while you play a game helps take your mind off all that.

principles.principle: Exercise at least a little regularly, even if you dislike it.
principles.why: People who exercise tend to be far more productive than people who don't.
principles.how: Build small home routines, such as adjustable dumbbells, when you can't get to a gym, and increase the load gradually.
principles.anti_pattern: Going overboard; he hurt his legs climbing around 500 stairs.
principles.quote: So it's better to exercise at least a little.

summary: Choose music whose tempo (BPM) matches the speed of the action and the mood of each scene, and treat tempo as a deliberate design decision.
takeaways: BPM counts beats per minute; one clap per second is 60
Smash battle music averages 130–170 BPM, rarely near 200
The right tempo depends on the action's speed
Different scenes within one game need different tempos

principles.principle: Match music tempo to the speed of the game's action.
principles.why: Some tempos fit a game's content and others don't; even among similar fighting games the right tempo varies with how fast the action is.
principles.how: Measure each track's BPM; for fast battles aim around 130–170 BPM, as Smash Bros. battle arrangements do, and treat ~200 BPM as an exception.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. battle stage music, 130–170 BPM on average.
principles.quote: Even among similar fighting games, the right tempo will vary depending on the speed of the action.

principles.principle: Vary tempo and rhythm between scenes within the same game.
principles.why: Different scenes in one game call for different tempos and rhythms, and tempo can reinforce what the player is going through.
principles.how: Assign a target tempo per scene; for example, slow the music as the player goes deeper into a dungeon, as the first Dragon Quest did.
principles.example: Dragon Quest, where dungeon music slows the deeper you go.
principles.quote: Of course, the same applies within one single game, where different scenes will call for certain tempos and rhythms.

summary: Game essence (push and pull, risk and reward) is only one source of fun, so identify what else your game's fun rests on, strengthen it, and add risk and reward where it fits.
takeaways: Game essence is only one of many sources of fun
Finely tuned control feel alone can carry a game
Story must use interactivity; story alone isn't enough
Simple sound cues make simulated worlds feel bigger
Add risk to crafting and rhythm games to deepen them

principles.principle: Identify which source of fun your game relies on beyond game essence.
principles.why: Fun comes from more than push and pull: control feel, story, fandom, simulation, creation and rhythm can each carry a game.
principles.how: Name your game's main source of fun and invest in it; for example, fine-tune control feel if controlling the character is the fun.
principles.anti_pattern: Assuming a compelling story alone is enough to make a good game.
principles.example: Ace Attorney, Animal Crossing, beatmania and a train simulator as fun beyond pure game essence.
principles.quote: Game essence isn't the only thing that makes a game fun

principles.principle: Layer risk and reward onto creation and timing-based play.
principles.why: Crafting is fun on its own, but dangers like falling, enemies or risky gathering can make it a lot more fun; strict timing keeps rhythm games tense.
principles.how: Add fall deaths, enemies that make building defenses matter, or dangerous resource trips; keep timing judgment strict enough that slightly late is a miss.
principles.anti_pattern: Loose judgment that gives Goods or Bads further from the note, reducing risk.
principles.example: beatmania, where a hair late counts as a miss.
principles.quote: there would be less risk involved, and people might find it a bit boring.

principles.principle: Use a few simple sounds to imply a world beyond the screen.
principles.why: As a game approaches real life, players perceive more information than is actually shown, which deepens the experience.
principles.how: Trigger a handful of simple, well-timed sound effects, like doors clattering and feet shuffling, to suggest offscreen activity.
principles.example: A train simulator arriving at a station.
principles.quote: All the program does is call a handful of simple sound effects, but it really feels like the doors are opening and people are getting on board

principles.principle: Use story and characters to drive players onward into risk.
principles.why: Stories aren't game essence but enhance it: they push players forward to face risks, and fleshed-out characters create a visceral connection.
principles.how: Tie story beats to the challenges ahead, and design stories that use interactivity rather than copying novels or films.
principles.anti_pattern: Relying on story alone without interactivity.
principles.quote: They're a driving force that keeps players pushing onward to face risks.

summary: Build a concept by naming a real problem in an existing genre and designing core rules that solve it, then prove the idea with a playable prototype.
takeaways: Smash was designed to restore push and pull lost to combos
Accumulated damage varies reactions; ring-outs decide matches
Direction-plus-button controls replaced complicated command inputs
Familiar Nintendo characters solved the unknown-roster problem
Flexible rules let players play what they want, how they want

principles.principle: Design your concept to solve a specific problem in its genre.
principles.why: He felt combo-focused fighters lost push and pull: after the first hit the opponent's skill was irrelevant and newcomers just watched themselves lose.
principles.how: List the genre's pain points, then design a core rule that removes them, as accumulated damage and ring-outs created room for interplay and improvisation.
principles.anti_pattern: Letting inputs alone decide the outcome after the first hit.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros.' accumulated damage system.
principles.quote: Instead of inputs alone determining the outcome, I wondered if we could make a game with more room for interplay and improvisation.

principles.principle: Keep controls to a stick direction plus a button.
principles.why: By 1996 fighting-game command inputs had become extremely complicated; simple inputs are something players can pick up intuitively.
principles.how: Map moves to direction plus button, and use input timing, such as a quick stick flick, to trigger stronger attacks or jumps.
principles.anti_pattern: Complex command inputs.
principles.example: The smash input, a flick of the N64 analog stick.
principles.quote: So I opted for simple controls with a stick direction and a button, something players could intuitively pick up.

principles.principle: Prototype the core rules first, and pick the concept you can finish.
principles.why: Prototypes of both concepts won praise from Nintendo; when the team urgently needed a finished game, the fighter could ship far sooner than the two-year RC game.
principles.how: Build a bare prototype with only the core rules, and estimate each concept's development time before choosing what to make.
principles.example: The Dragon King: The Fighting Game prototype.
principles.quote: There were no special moves, dodges, or even items yet, but the game's rules were basically the same as Smash Bros., as you can see.

principles.principle: Give players a reason to care about a large cast immediately.
principles.why: Console fighting games can launch with 8 or even 12 new main characters at once, and it's hard to make someone care about them.
principles.how: Use characters players already know, or build ways for attachment to grow, as arcades do through watching others play.
principles.anti_pattern: A roster full of characters nobody has seen.
principles.example: Smash borrowing Nintendo's most popular characters.
principles.quote: For the customer, that's 12 new faces who just showed up out of nowhere.

summary: Exaggerate attack poses past what looks "OK," pushing rigs to their limits and overshooting before settling, because on a small screen merely adequate motion reads as weak.
takeaways: Too much is just right for attack animations
If a pose looks OK, push it even further
Don't correct poses that only look warped when paused
Overshoot one frame, then pull back

principles.principle: Exaggerate attack poses until they nearly break the rig.
principles.why: Attacks are small on a small screen, so the usual problem is not going far enough; if a pose looks OK, there's room to go further.
principles.how: Push twists and extensions past natural limits, and build flexible rigs (moving shoulders, independent upper and lower body) that allow it.
principles.anti_pattern: Keeping poses within the physically possible.
principles.example: Kazuya's Roundhouse to Triple Spin Kick; Virtua Fighter's opposed upper and lower body.
principles.quote: Animation that pushes your rig's weighting to the breaking point is good animation.

principles.principle: Judge animation in motion, not by warped-looking paused frames.
principles.why: Correcting a model that looks warped when the action is stopped kills the energy of the animation.
principles.how: Review attacks at full speed and in-game size, and reject fixes for distortions that only show up in freeze-frames.
principles.anti_pattern: Smoothing out deformations that are only visible when paused.
principles.quote: Sometimes a model looks warped when the action is stopped, and we're asked to make corrections, but that really kills the energy of the animation.

principles.principle: Overshoot the target pose, then pull back on the next frame.
principles.why: Going past the natural limit and then pulling back makes even linear animation livelier; he has used it since the NES days.
principles.how: In a frame sequence, place one frame beyond the final pose and settle back to that pose on the following frame.
principles.example: Kirby's Adventure's Needle ability, where frame three goes too far and frame four pulls back.
principles.quote: This also works with linear animations— go over the natural limit, then pull back a bit.

summary: Avoid mid-development spec changes by planning for fun from the start, but when change is unavoidable, surface problems immediately, put every option on the table, and decide fast.
takeaways: Avoid spec changes, but stay flexible when they're needed
Never change course because it isn't fun; plan fun early
Raise problems immediately; hindsight complaints help nobody
Gather all options, then decide fast with full information

principles.principle: Plan for fun from the start so fun never forces a spec change.
principles.why: Spec changes scrap finished work, cost money and hurt morale; changing course because the game isn't fun is the one to avoid.
principles.how: Validate the core fun during planning, before committing production work to it.
principles.anti_pattern: Discovering mid-production that the game isn't fun.
principles.quote: What you really want to avoid is having to change course because your game's not fun.

principles.principle: Report problems the moment you spot them, with everything you know.
principles.why: Players can't fix what's wrong but the team can, and the sooner problems are raised, the less time is wasted.
principles.how: Make it a team rule that anyone tells the lead right away and shares all their information without debating how to phrase it.
principles.anti_pattern: Saying "I knew that was wrong!" after the fact.
principles.quote: As soon as you spot an issue, you have to tell someone right away.

principles.principle: Put every option on the table, then decide quickly.
principles.why: Long deliberation wastes time, but decisions need accurate information, and collective knowledge beats any one person's.
principles.how: Gather all known facts and options, pick the one that works short- and long-term, and decide immediately.
principles.anti_pattern: Digging in your heels on an idea that isn't working.
principles.quote: The moment a problem crops up, I make a decision immediately rather than spending time on it.

principles.principle: Don't try to spec the entire finished game before building.
principles.why: Some things only become clear once you make the game, and full up-front documentation can take as long as development itself.
principles.how: Spec enough to start, then refine details as implementation reveals them.
principles.anti_pattern: Writing documentation for the whole finished game from the get-go.

summary: Make terrain with collision stand out and tone down non-colliding backdrop so players always know where solid ground is, while keeping the stage attractive and giving gameplay the slight edge.
takeaways: Players must always know where solid ground is
Emphasize collision objects; de-emphasize the backdrop
Aerial perspective helps, but alone it hurts the look
Balance looks and gameplay, favoring gameplay slightly

principles.principle: Make colliding terrain stand out more than the backdrop.
principles.why: In action games players must always know where solid ground is, and 3D perspective makes collision hard to recognize.
principles.how: Give non-terrain elements less emphasis, for example with aerial perspective, and check that terrain reads first during play.
principles.anti_pattern: A backdrop that outshines the terrain.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. stages.
principles.quote: Make the objects with collision stand out— and give the backdrop less emphasis.

principles.principle: Balance readability and looks, giving gameplay the slight edge.
principles.why: Some say visuals are irrelevant to gameplay, but that won't matter if nobody buys the game; still, gameplay clarity should get the slight edge.
principles.how: Don't just fade out everything that isn't terrain; keep backgrounds attractive while ensuring terrain dominates.
principles.anti_pattern: Applying aerial perspective alone and hurting the overall look.
principles.quote: It's all about striking a balance, though I'd say it's best to give gameplay the slight edge.

principles.principle: Make sure artists understand each asset's role in gameplay.
principles.why: An artist's job isn't just producing artwork; the art has to suit its function in the game.
principles.how: Brief artists on which elements are collidable, and review their art in gameplay context rather than as standalone pictures.
principles.anti_pattern: Treating art as standalone pieces.
principles.quote: An artist's job isn't just producing artwork and calling it a day— understand your art's role in the game and make what's appropriate!

summary: Games are remarkably cheap for the hours of fun they give and the size of the teams behind them, so if there's a game you want to play or support, buy it or play it through a subscription.
takeaways: Games offer dozens of hours of fun for $70 or less
Game scope grew tens to hundreds of times; prices barely moved
Subscriptions cover costs but pit new games against older ones
Buy or subscribe to support creators

principles.principle: Weigh subscription deals: covered costs versus competing with older titles.
principles.why: Subscriptions bring the joy of having production costs covered, but also the pain of competing with older titles in the same catalog.
principles.how: When deciding whether to release through a subscription service, count both the cost coverage and the competition from the back catalog.
principles.quote: There's the joy of having your production costs covered, but also the pain of competing with older titles.

principles.principle: Support the creators of games you want by buying or subscribing.
principles.why: Games need large teams plus marketing and release costs, yet prices have stayed flat, and a game's price means little if nobody plays it.
principles.how: Buy the game, or play it through a subscription, instead of hesitating.
principles.quote: At the end of the day, the price of a game doesn't mean much if nobody plays it.

summary: Set each sound effect's volume by how relevant it is to the player, not by how big the action is, building a clear priority order from match-deciding events down to footsteps.
takeaways: Volume should follow relevance to the player, not action size
In Smash, KO sounds are loudest, then hits
Landings are louder than jumps; footsteps vary per character
Use sound variations to avoid mechanical repetition
Audible footsteps keep 3D characters from seeming to hover

principles.principle: Make sounds louder the more relevant they are to the player.
principles.why: Match-deciding events and direct feedback for the player's actions matter most; judging only by the size of an action can give the wrong result.
principles.how: Rank effects (KO > hits > specials and voices > dodges and blocks > swings > landing > jump > walk) and mix in that order.
principles.anti_pattern: Setting volume by the action's physical size alone.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros.' sound priority order.
principles.quote: The more relevant a sound is to the player, the louder that sound should be.

principles.principle: Make landing sounds louder than jump sounds.
principles.why: Landing is a reaction, so it gets more emphasis than the jump that caused it.
principles.how: Mix landings above jumps, and give each character landing sounds that match their clothing or footwear.
principles.example: Cloud's landing sounds, which differ by costume.
principles.quote: Since landing is a reaction, we make it louder than the jump.

principles.principle: Make footsteps audible and varied by character and floor.
principles.why: Barely audible footsteps make characters feel like they're hovering, one repeated effect sounds mechanical, and believable sounds feel best.
principles.how: Record several footstep variants per character and per floor material, and rotate between them.
principles.anti_pattern: Silent or single-sample footsteps.
principles.example: Unique footsteps for every Smash fighter.
principles.quote: You can barely hear them in a lot of games, making it feel like something is missing— as if your character is hovering, not walking.

summary: Size and lay out text for each language (kanji need bigger characters, alphabetic text needs more length) and check it on the real target screen so it is never too small.
takeaways: Appropriate text size varies from language to language
Kanji need bigger characters; English needs more letters
Leave layout flexibility for translations
Check text on the actual handheld screen
Font-size options are extremely accommodating

principles.principle: Size and lay out text per language, not just for English.
principles.why: Kanji need larger characters but fewer of them, English is legible small but runs longer, and French longer still; English-only layouts leave translations too small.
principles.how: Leave flexible room in every text area for each target language's glyph size and string length.
principles.anti_pattern: Designing the layout with only English in mind.
principles.example: Japanese, English and French text compared.
principles.quote: This is something I'd like to impress on developers both in Japan and abroad: the appropriate text size will vary from language to language.

principles.principle: Check text size on the actual target screen.
principles.why: Handheld developers who check their game on the actual device quickly spot text that's too small, which is why handheld games tend to use larger fonts.
principles.how: Review every UI screen on the real hardware, in each language, during development.
principles.example: Nintendo Switch handheld games.
principles.quote: They'll spot it quickly if the text is too small.

principles.principle: Offer a player-selectable font size when screen space allows.
principles.why: Letting players choose the font size is extremely accommodating, and a clean interface leaves the screen space to support it.
principles.how: Keep the interface uncluttered and add a font-size setting, while keeping even the largest size reasonably stylish.
principles.anti_pattern: Text so big it no longer looks stylish.
principles.quote: Some games even let you choose the font size for yourself.

summary: The quickest way into making games for a living is to make a game yourself: finish it, get people to play it, learn from their reactions, and show originality when you apply.
takeaways: Quickest way into games: make a game yourself
Mimicking existing games is fine when starting out
Let others play it and learn from reactions
Apply with your game even without every requirement
Originality sets you apart from other applicants

principles.principle: Make and finish your own game to break into the industry.
principles.why: It's the quickest, if not only, way in: you see which problems arise and how to solve them, and even designers need to think like programmers.
principles.how: Pick any tool (Unity, Unreal Engine, JavaScript, Maker software) and start small; mimicking an existing game is fine at first.
principles.quote: For starters, just take a shot at making your own game.

principles.principle: Get people to play your game and act on their feedback.
principles.why: Players' reactions show what to improve or what to carry into the next project, and distributing a game can also teach PR.
principles.how: Ask friends, distribute it free online, or sell it if confident; then revise the game or apply the lessons next time.
principles.quote: And once people play your game, find out what they think— and either go back and make improvements, or carry that experience and knowledge into your next project.

principles.principle: Show originality in the game you submit with applications.
principles.why: Many people want to make games; companies want people who can make fun games, and an imitative idea won't help your case.
principles.how: Send a game with an original idea along with your application, even if you don't meet every listed requirement.
principles.anti_pattern: Submitting an imitative game idea.
principles.quote: That said, an imitative game idea won't do much to help your case. Find a way to let your originality shine.

summary: Shape effects so the character stays visible inside them, through gaps, effect geometry that varies by viewing side, and outlines, rather than letting a big effect bury the character in 3D.
takeaways: Characters easily get lost in big effects, especially in 3D
In 2D, simply draw characters above effects
Forced 3D draw priority causes depth disparity
Shape effects to leave characters partially visible
Outlines help characters stand out

principles.principle: Keep characters visible inside their own effects.
principles.why: Effects are needed for impact, but characters easily get lost in them, especially in 3D views that aren't overhead.
principles.how: Shape effects so the character stays at least partially visible, like Terry inside the Power Dunk crown or Captain Falcon in the Falcon Punch.
principles.anti_pattern: Effects that completely bury the character.
principles.example: Terry's Power Dunk and Captain Falcon's Falcon Punch in Super Smash Bros.
principles.quote: Though it's tough to avoid if you want to leave an impact, sometimes characters can get lost in a sea of special effects.

principles.principle: Vary effect geometry by viewing side so it doesn't block characters.
principles.why: Making the parts of an effect different heights from the front and back keeps it from obstructing the character in the middle.
principles.how: For effects that surround a character, shape the camera-facing parts differently from the far side so the character remains visible.
principles.example: The inner blue peaks of Chrom's Up Special.
principles.quote: If you look at the inner blue peaks, you'll notice they're a different height when viewed from the front or back.

principles.principle: In 3D, avoid forced draw priority; fix visibility with shapes and outlines.
principles.why: In 2D characters can simply draw over effects, but forcing that in 3D usually creates depth disparity that looks bad.
principles.how: Solve visibility through effect shapes, and add an outline around character models.
principles.anti_pattern: Forcing characters to render above 3D effects.
principles.quote: In a 3D game, it's possible to forcibly give the characters higher display priority, but more often than not this creates depth disparity, and just doesn't look that great.

summary: Structure every attack as standby, lead-in, attack and follow-through: snap instantly into a big lead-in pose, freeze the hit with hitstop, hold a distinct follow-through, and add cancel frames.
takeaways: Attacks: standby, lead-in, attack, follow-through
Jump instantly to the lead-in pose to confirm input
Hitstop makes the hit pose firm and readable
Hold a distinct follow-through, then allow cancel frames
Spec standby, attack pose, start frame and total frames

principles.principle: Snap to a big lead-in pose on the attack's first frame.
principles.why: A smooth transition from standby takes too long; an instant big pose tells the player the input registered and cues the opponent to dodge.
principles.how: Skip easing frames out of standby and make frame one of the attack a big windup pose.
principles.anti_pattern: Gradual transitions into the windup.
principles.quote: By instantly jumping to a big pose, the player can immediately know their input was recognized.

principles.principle: Hold a distinct follow-through, then let cancel frames return control.
principles.why: The follow-through is the opening when the player can't act, so it must read clearly; returning control only at standby felt heavy or rigid.
principles.how: Make the follow-through look clearly unlike standby and hold it, and add cancel frames so players can move, jump or attack early.
principles.anti_pattern: Returning control only once the character is back in standby.
principles.example: Smash Bros. through Melee, before cancel frames.
principles.quote: The player can't control the character here, so we keep this pose very distinct from the standby pose, and hold it as long as possible.

principles.principle: Spec attacks by standby pose, attack pose, start frame and total frames.
principles.why: The lead-in and follow-through fit between those markers, so these four facts give animators a good starting point.
principles.how: In every animation request, list the standby pose, the attack key pose, the frame the hit starts, and total frames until cancelable.
principles.quote: The standby pose. The attack pose. The attack start frame. and the total frames— or the time until the attack can be canceled.

principles.principle: Use hitstop to freeze the hit into a readable key pose.
principles.why: Everything hinges on the moment an attack can hit; stopping the animation on contact makes that pose firm and readable.
principles.how: Pause the animation when a hit lands so the attack pose holds on screen.
principles.quote: You could say everything hinges on this moment.

summary: Build jumps from an initial upward velocity plus per-frame downward acceleration, then shape the rise, fall, air control and windup to fit what your game needs.
takeaways: Jumps: initial upward velocity plus per-frame downward acceleration
Rise and fall speeds define a jump's feel
Faster falls add impact to slams
A short pre-jump windup keeps Up Smash inputs possible
Ultimate's burst-then-brake jump forgives late reactions

principles.principle: Shape the jump's rise, fall and air control to your game's goals.
principles.why: Mario's gentle rise and fast fall suits variable height, Samus's floaty jump helps with aiming, and Ghosts 'n Goblins' fixed arc makes every jump a plan.
principles.how: Tune separate rise and fall acceleration and air control for what your game needs rather than using default physics.
principles.anti_pattern: One generic jump for every game.
principles.example: Super Mario Bros., Metroid and Ghosts 'n Goblins.
principles.quote: Remember, though: your jump might change depending on the goal of your game.

principles.principle: Make descents faster than ascents to add impact.
principles.why: Even with the same trajectory, adjusting a move's speed drastically changes how it feels.
principles.how: For slams, throws or heavy landings, increase downward acceleration on the way down.
principles.example: Zangief's Spinning Pile Driver from Street Fighter II Turbo onward.
principles.quote: Even with the same trajectory, adjusting a move's speed can drastically change how it feels.

principles.principle: Keep a short, uniform windup before jumps when up-attacks share the input.
principles.why: Without the windup, players would jump before they could input an Up Smash.
principles.how: Add a short pre-jump windup and use the same length for every character.
principles.anti_pattern: Removing the windup entirely.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros.' unified jump windup.
principles.quote: If we removed it entirely, players would end up jumping before they could input an Up Smash— so we have to keep it in some form.

principles.principle: Use a strong burst, then brief heavy gravity, for forgiving escape jumps.
principles.why: Players can still get out of a jam even if they react a little late; the extra parameters and bug risk are worth it.
principles.how: Apply very strong initial upward velocity, greatly increase downward acceleration for a few frames until the jump halts, then restore normal gravity.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate and Kirby Super Star.
principles.quote: This way, players can still get out of a jam even if they react a little late.

summary: Build proposals as fast-moving slides, one image and two lines of text per page, grouped into categories, and talk around them instead of reading them aloud.
takeaways: One screenshot and two lines of text per page
Many pages are fine if each moves quickly
Use categories so people know their progress
Don't read wall-of-text slides aloud
Content matters most

principles.principle: Use one image and two lines of text per proposal page.
principles.why: Single-topic pages read quickly like comic panels, so even a 200-plus-page deck doesn't take long to present.
principles.how: Build each slide around one screenshot or diagram and two lines of text, with one topic per slide.
principles.example: The Super Smash Bros. Ultimate proposal (200+ pages).
principles.quote: One screenshot or diagram, and just two lines of text.

principles.principle: Organize proposals into categories so listeners know where they are.
principles.why: People can follow along and see how far into the presentation they are, and nobody likes an endless presentation.
principles.how: Group slides into categories and subcategories with clear section markers.
principles.anti_pattern: A long deck with no visible structure.
principles.quote: Nobody likes an endless presentation, after all.

principles.principle: Talk around your slides; never read them aloud.
principles.why: Slides that are a wall of text read out loud are annoying, and people just read ahead.
principles.how: Keep slide text minimal and say a little about each slide in your own words.
principles.anti_pattern: Reading a wall of text straight off the page.
principles.quote: It can be pretty annoying when a slide is just a wall of text the presenter reads out loud.

summary: A game-free break in which Sakurai answers fans' repeated requests for more of his cat, Fukurashi; the only lesson is that it's worth giving your audience what they keep asking for.
takeaways: Game-free Grab Bag episode about his cat Fukurashi
Followers of his daily Smash screens asked for more cat posts
Her name is Fukura; Fukurashi rolls off the tongue

principles.principle: When followers keep asking for something, give them dedicated content.
principles.why: Followers of his daily Smash Bros. screens kept begging for more of his cat, so he devoted a whole video to her.
principles.how: Note recurring requests from your audience, even off-topic ones, and answer them with a dedicated post or video.
principles.example: His daily Smash Bros. screens on Twitter, where people asked for more cat posts.
principles.quote: All that time I spent posting daily Smash Bros. screens on Twitter, there was one thing people begged me to post even more of.

summary: A sequel's concept can simply be "power up everything": use the new hardware's headroom to upgrade every element, and add the special touches that set the game apart.
takeaways: Melee's concept: power up Smash Bros. by leaps and bounds
N64 fighters had about 300 polygons and 64x64 textures
Streaming audio enabled orchestral arrangements
Trophies added Nintendo characters beyond the roster
Creative works must set themselves apart

principles.principle: For a sequel, upgrade every element substantially, not just a few.
principles.why: Melee's concept was simply to power up Smash by leaps and bounds, and upgrading fighters, stages, graphics, sound, play feel and more made it eye-opening.
principles.how: List all of the game's elements and set a clear upgrade goal for each, using the new hardware's headroom.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. Melee on GameCube.
principles.quote: That was, of course, to power up Smash Bros. by leaps and bounds!

principles.principle: Use collectibles to include franchise characters you can't make playable.
principles.why: There was a limit to how many fighters fit, but trophies brought other Nintendo characters in, with background info as fan service.
principles.how: Add a collection with short background entries for characters who didn't make the playable roster.
principles.example: Melee's Trophy system.
principles.quote: There was a limit to how many fighters we could include in the game, but this gave us a way to bring together other characters from across Nintendo's history

principles.principle: Make the extra effort that sets your work apart.
principles.why: Most creative works have to do what they can to stand out from the crowd, even when the labor is immense.
principles.how: Identify the touches that will make your game feel extra special, like orchestral music or a CG movie, and commit to them.
principles.example: Melee's orchestral arrangements and first CG movie.
principles.quote: Still, I'd say most creative works— not just games— have to do what they can to set themselves apart from the crowd.

summary: Let players bet resources on higher difficulty for bigger rewards and ease off automatically after failure, but make sure newcomers understand how to turn the difficulty down.
takeaways: Pay hearts to raise Intensity for bigger rewards
Failing spills hearts and automatically lowers difficulty
Intensity 0.0 makes the player nearly invincible
Risk and reward can make games feel too hardcore
Tell beginners clearly how to lower difficulty
games: Super Smash Bros. for Wii U/3DS

principles.principle: Let players wager currency on difficulty for proportionally bigger rewards.
principles.why: A big risk for a big reward creates game essence and rewards strong play, which ordinary difficulty settings don't.
principles.how: Charge currency to raise intensity, boost enemy aggression, attack and defense, and pay out more currency and better items on a clear.
principles.example: Kid Icarus: Uprising's Fiend's Cauldron.
principles.quote: If you take a big risk, you can get a big reward.

principles.principle: Lower difficulty automatically after failure instead of offering Easy Mode.
principles.why: Players rarely get stuck, it stings less than bluntly asking them to switch to Easy, and nobody has to play the whole game on Easy.
principles.how: When an attempt fails, reduce the difficulty for the retry and take part of the player's stake as the cost.
principles.anti_pattern: Bluntly prompting failing players to switch to Easy Mode.
principles.example: Hearts spilling from the Fiend's Cauldron on failure.
principles.quote: The system automatically lowers the difficulty when you fail, so the player rarely gets stuck.

principles.principle: Clearly teach beginners how to lower the difficulty.
principles.why: Players weren't told clearly enough that going below Intensity 2.0 lowered difficulty, and newcomers needed that most.
principles.how: Introduce the lower-difficulty option explicitly to new players, not just the high-risk end.
principles.anti_pattern: Leaving the easy side of a difficulty system unexplained.
principles.example: Kid Icarus: Uprising's Intensity below 2.0.
principles.quote: Newcomers to the game are the ones who needed this most.

principles.principle: Balance risk-and-reward systems against approachability.
principles.why: Game essence makes games gamelike but can make them less approachable, especially on a small screen; constant pressure feels too hardcore.
principles.how: Check stage length, enemy density and respawn points so the risk system doesn't make the whole game feel hardcore.
principles.anti_pattern: Stages too big, with too many enemies, and no respawn where you died.
principles.example: Kid Icarus: Uprising's land stages.
principles.quote: Game essence, push and pull, and risk and reward are great for making the experience "gamelike," but they can conversely make games feel less approachable, too.

summary: The screen is a small window (about 30 degrees of the player's vision) into your game's world, so decide deliberately how much of it your gameplay and targets occupy.
takeaways: Screens fill only about 30 degrees of vision
Cockpit views cost playable screen space
VR blurs distance but suits separate gaze and heading
Tiny FPS targets lack impact; enlarge enemies

principles.principle: Budget how much of the screen your gameplay actually uses.
principles.why: The screen covers only about 30 degrees of vision, so a wide view is squeezed into a narrow window and screen space is scarce.
principles.how: Choose camera views that leave more room for play, and avoid views like cockpit cameras that shrink the usable area.
principles.anti_pattern: Picking the most realistic camera at the cost of playable screen space.
principles.example: Cockpit views in racing games.
principles.quote: Back to the topic at hand, it's important to think about just how much screen space you're using for your gameplay.

principles.principle: Scale up targets that look too small on screen.
principles.why: In first-person shooters the target is tiny compared with the screen, which lacks some impact as entertainment.
principles.how: Make enemies several times bigger than the player character, as in Kid Icarus: Uprising, if it fits what you're going for.
principles.example: Kid Icarus: Uprising's oversized enemies.
principles.quote: In Kid Icarus: Uprising, I compensated for this by making enemies several times bigger than the player, but it really depends on what you're going for.

principles.principle: Use VR where viewpoint and direction of travel are separate.
principles.why: VR's lower resolution blurs distant objects and you must turn your whole head, but it's a perfect fit when you look somewhere other than where you're moving.
principles.how: Weigh the resolution and head-turning costs, and favor VR for games like racing where gaze and heading differ.
principles.example: VR racing.
principles.quote: Motion sickness is always a possibility, but for games that separate your viewpoint and direction of travel, VR is truly the perfect fit.

summary: Keep every team member connected to the whole game with regular shared information (a daily report, a daily screenshot and periodic team presentations) so nobody feels like a cog.
takeaways: Working without the big picture is stressful
Daily Report: a development newspaper with comments
Screenshot of the Day shares progress and builds fun
Periodic team presentations prevent feeling like cogs

principles.principle: Keep a daily report page the whole team can read and comment on.
principles.why: On large games people lose sight of what they're making, and working without the larger picture is stressful.
principles.how: Post progress, news and your thoughts on the project every day, like a development newspaper, with a comment field for the team.
principles.example: Sakurai's Daily Report.
principles.quote: But working like that—without a clear vision of the larger picture—is stressful, in my opinion.

principles.principle: Share one in-progress screenshot with the team every day.
principles.why: It shows everyone where the game stands, including content unfit for the public, and writing captions in the comments helps the team unwind.
principles.how: Attach a daily screenshot to the report page and invite comments and captions.
principles.example: Screenshot of the Day, later repurposed for his daily screens on Twitter.
principles.quote: The team really enjoyed coming up with captions for these in the comments, so it was a nice way to unwind.

principles.principle: Hold cross-discipline progress presentations every few months.
principles.why: Everyone gets a broader view of the project instead of feeling like mere cogs, plus motivation and a sense of accomplishment.
principles.how: Have each team (graphics, sound, animation, VFX, UI) present its work to everyone, despite scheduling and venue hassles.
principles.anti_pattern: Skipping them because they're a hassle to organize.
principles.example: Project Presentations on Sakurai's teams.
principles.quote: By having the teams present their progress, everyone gets a broader view of the project instead of feeling like mere cogs in a machine.

summary: Spend limited performance and labor on what players actually look at (screen center, playable surfaces, assets shown up close) and cut detail nobody will ever see.
takeaways: Hardware is weaker than most people think, so economize
Players mostly look at the screen center
Prioritize by screen coverage and every place an asset appears
LOD must be worth its labor
Cut details truly nobody will see

principles.principle: Put performance and detail where players are actually looking.
principles.why: Hardware is weaker than people think, and players mostly look at the screen center and the playable surfaces.
principles.how: Detail the area in front of the camera and the stage surface; simplify the rest of the skysphere and off-screen foundations.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. skyspheres and stage terrain.
principles.quote: But the place players are most likely to be looking is the center of the screen.

principles.principle: Budget assets by on-screen size and every context they appear in.
principles.why: Elements shown small in play don't need lavish detail, but models also shown up close in other assets need more.
principles.how: Estimate each element's screen coverage in play, factor in its other close-up uses, then assign its budget.
principles.anti_pattern: Lavishing detail on elements that are small on screen.
principles.example: Smash fighters versus stages.
principles.quote: It's important to consider how much of the screen each element takes up.

principles.principle: Cut detail nobody will see, but allow harmless playfulness.
principles.why: A bit of playfulness makes the game better if it meets deadlines and doesn't hurt performance, but invisible details waste resources.
principles.how: Approve small extras that don't affect schedule or frame rate; ask the team to tone down ones no player will ever notice.
principles.anti_pattern: Animating details truly nobody will see.
principles.example: Turning car tires in the backdrop of Inkling's stage.
principles.quote: It was something truly nobody would see.

principles.principle: Build LOD only when the performance gain justifies the labor.
principles.why: LOD swaps in lower-polygon assets with distance, but it's labor-intensive.
principles.how: Estimate the performance gain against the authoring cost before committing to LOD models.
principles.anti_pattern: Building LOD by default.
principles.quote: But implementing this is labor-intensive, so the performance benefit needs to be worth it.

summary: Don't hold modern games to nostalgic standards: fun is relative to its time and circumstances, so keep trying new things and enjoy the present.
takeaways: Nostalgia makes old games the wrong standard
Fun is relative to time, situation, trends and tech
Modern games offer more total fun and breadth
Older games had more room to experiment
Keep trying new things

principles.principle: Keep playing new games instead of judging by nostalgic standards.
principles.why: Works from our youth leave deep imprints, and it's a shame to bounce off modern games just because they can't match those memories.
principles.how: Regularly try new titles and expand beyond what you already like.
principles.anti_pattern: Treating old games as the standard all others are held to.
principles.quote: It's better to keep trying new things, right?

principles.principle: Judge fun as relative to its time and context.
principles.why: The year you play, your personal situation, trends and technology all greatly affect how much fun a game is.
principles.how: Replay an old game today next to a recent one before deciding which is better.
principles.anti_pattern: Comparing a modern game against your memory of an old one.
principles.quote: The fun of a game isn't based in absolutes. It's more of a relative thing.

summary: Move every tunable value out of code into designer-editable parameters, with formulas, hidden rarely used fields and one-button conversion to running builds, so tuning iterations are fast.
takeaways: Code is bones; parameters are muscles
Keep tunable values in a separate spreadsheet
Hide rarely used parameters; link others with formulas
One-button conversion to all dev kits speeds iteration
Early Smash conversions took ten minutes per tweak
games: Super Smash Bros. for Wii U/3DS

principles.principle: Separate every tunable value from code into designer-editable parameters.
principles.why: Hard-coding means diving into code for every tweak, causing real problems; parameters let designers make the same code behave very differently.
principles.how: Have programmers read values like attack power from a parameter table kept in a separate spreadsheet.
principles.anti_pattern: Writing tunable numbers directly into code.
principles.example: A move with attack power 10 stored as a parameter.
principles.quote: You could say the code is the bones, and the parameters are the muscles.

principles.principle: Hide rarely used parameters and link related ones with formulas.
principles.why: Hiding reduces human error and surfaces the important values; formulas keep related values in relative balance.
principles.how: Collapse low-frequency fields in the editor, and define dependent values, such as one move at 1/2 another's power.
principles.example: Smash Bros. attack parameters in Excel.
principles.quote: This helps reduce human error and makes it easier to find the important values, so hiding the parameters you don't use often is an effective approach.

principles.principle: Push parameter changes to all test builds with one button.
principles.why: Tuning is where you iterate most; ten-minute conversions plus reboots on early Smash games made every tweak costly.
principles.how: Build a tool, such as a spreadsheet add-in, that converts parameters and updates every active dev kit in one press.
principles.anti_pattern: Slow conversions and hand-edited text files.
principles.example: Original Smash and Melee versus Wii U/3DS onward with Bandai Namco Studios.
principles.quote: This is the area where you'll likely need to iterate the most, so make sure your team can do so as efficiently as possible.

principles.principle: Let more team members adjust parameters easily.
principles.why: When more people can adjust values, trial and error is easy and more values get tuned more deeply; early on, Sakurai wrote every parameter himself.
principles.how: Store parameters in an accessible format so designers beyond the lead can tune them.
principles.anti_pattern: A single person as the only one who can change values.
principles.example: Smash Bros. for Wii U/3DS onward.
principles.quote: our parameters are maintained in a way that lets more people adjust them easily
